description_full: The Coca-Cola Company, a beverage company, manufactures and sells various nonalcoholic beverages in the United States and internationally. The company provides Trademark Coca-Cola, sparkling soft drinks and flavors; water, sports, coffee, and tea; juice, value-added dairy, and plant-based beverages; and emerging beverages. It also offers beverage concentrates and syrups, as well as fountain syrups to fountain retailers comprising restaurants and convenience stores. The company sells its products under the Coca-Cola, Diet Coke/Coca-Cola Light, Coca-Cola Zero Sugar, caffeine free Diet Coke, Cherry Coke, Fanta, Sprite, Simply, Fanta Orange, Fanta Zero Orange, Fanta Zero Sugar, Fanta Apple, Sprite Zero Sugar, Simply Orange, Simply Apple, Simply Grapefruit, Fresca, Schweppes, Thums Up, Aquarius, Ayataka, BODYARMOR, Ciel, Costa, Crystal, Dasani, Fuze Tea, Georgia, glacéau smartwater, glacéau vitaminwater, Gold Peak, I LOHAS, Powerade, Topo Chico, Core Power, Del Valle, fairlife, innocent, Maaza, Minute Maid, Minute Maid Pulpy, Santa Clara, and dogadan brands. It operates through a network of independent bottling partners, distributors, wholesalers, and retailers, as well as through bottling and distribution operators. The Coca-Cola Company was founded in 1886 and is headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia.

financial_summary: Coca-Cola Company (The) is a mega-cap consumer defensive business with a $411.6B market cap on $47.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 17% against a 6% cost of capital, a 10-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it. Gross margins of 61% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $5.3B in free cash flow — roughly 11 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.57×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.0× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 8.3×.

Shareholder yield of 2.2% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 9.9% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 3.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 163% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 3 other valuation measures)
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $158.4M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Slow-motion taste and channel shifts — private label, Gen-Z health preferences, or a DTC disruption can erode decade-old brand moats without a single dramatic quarter.
Input cost inflation from agricultural commodities — when raw materials spike, pass-through pricing lags and margin compression is immediate.
GLP-1 and health-trend demand destruction — weight-loss drugs and wellness shifts are structurally reducing consumption in snack, beverage, and packaged food categories.

sect: Its 29% operating margin runs 22pp above the Consumer Defensive median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 3.56x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 1.4% of sector revenue and 5.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+5.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 28% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 2% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 19% and a beta of 0.38, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $1.4B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 37% in the 2020 crash, 17% in the 2022 bear market and 41% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $36.40 (margin of safety -163%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 19%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $27.08 to $50.90 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 28.2 vs 18.5, EV/EBITDA 25.2 vs 10.3 and P/FCF 77.7 vs 16.0 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 41% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 24 covering analysts target $97.75 on average, 2% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 17% clears the cost of capital of 6.5% by 10pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.28).
It runs a 61% gross margin and converts 11% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: cash conversion of only 0.57x.
ROE of 41% is amplified by 3.3x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.6% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.0x net debt to EBITDA ($13.9B of cash against $43.6B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 8.3x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 5.5, in the safe zone).
The Beneish M-score (-2.20) sits just under the manipulation line, so earnings quality bears watching.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.7% over 3 years, 7.7% over 5 years and 0.8% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 12%).
At current returns, reinvesting 89% of profits supports about 14.8% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -9.4% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs 2.0x depreciation (4.4% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 18, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 4.0% on average.
own: Insiders own 9.9%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 68%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (26 sales, net $158.4M sold).
It returns 2.2% a year to shareholders (0.1% in buybacks and 2.2% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 64 consecutive years, raising it 4.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 65,900 employees, each generates about $727K of revenue, 1.4x the Consumer Defensive median, and productivity has risen 2.8% a year.
That works out to $80K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.2M (6x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
